newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Bruton seek IRA truce, see quick talks.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Bruton seek IRA truce, see quick talks.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and Irish Prime Minister John Bruton on Tuesday urged the IRA to declare a ceasefire in Northern Ireland, saying it would clear the way for its political arm, Sinn Fein, to join peace talks.
"We can't make peace until we end violence," Clinton told reporters in the Oval Office during the start of talks with Bruton on peace efforts in the troubled province.
The Irish Republican Army abandoned a 17-month truce last February, accusing Britain of refusing to allow Sinn Fein a voice in all-party political talks on the future of Northern Ireland.

"I want to reiterate my call for the IRA to institute a ceasefire in words as well as deeds," Clinton said. "If they do that I am convinced that Sinn Fein will be invited to participate in the talks."
"Peace will not come in the presence of violence," Clinton said. "It must come with the absence of violence."
Bruton said the IRA should agree to a ceasefire now rather than wait for the outcome of British elections next year because a new government in London could have a new policy toward Northern Ireland.

Britain's opposition Labour and Liberal Democrat parties said on Tuesday they would end cooperation with the ruling Conservatives in January -- making it difficult for Prime Minister John Major to remain in power.
Bruton said that "from every point of view" it would be better for the IRA to institute an immediate ceasefire. "We believe there is a major window of opportunity now."
During an exchange with reporters after the meeting, Bruton said he was not suggesting that Major was doomed to defeat when elections are held next year.
"Any election contains the possibility of a change of government," he said.
"There's a better opportunity to be derived by the republican movement with a ceasefire if they have it now than if they wait until after the elections," Bruton said.
"After the elections, whether there's a change of government or not, there will be a greater fixing of position and less fluidity than there is at the moment," he said.
Hopes for a new truce received a setback recently when Major rejected proposals from Catholic moderate leader John Hume aimed at speeding access to the talks by Sinn Fein.

London and Dublin agree the IRA must declare a ceasefire before Sinn Fein can join the talks but a meeting between Bruton and Major earlier this month failed to resolve how quickly the talks would be expanded.
Major says his intelligence agencies must determine whether any new IRA cessation is genuine and intended to last, unlike the first which Britain says was tactical.
Ireland is opposed to a lengthy delay in bringing Sinn Fein to the table once it has publicly accepted non-violence and an IRA truce is deemed to be credible.

Clinton, asked for his views on how quickly Sinn Fein should be allowed to participate if a ceasefire was declared, said: "I believe that Sinn Fein would be invited to participate in the talks fairly soon thereafter."

White House officials declined to be specific about Clinton's views on timing. "On this question, as on many others here, we've found it best to give our advice to the parties and to confer with them and not to try to give advice publicly," said spokesman David Johnson.
Clinton has elevated U.S. efforts in trying to bring an end to the violence that has plagued Northern Ireland. Last December, he became the first American president to visit the troubled province.
